Your answer has several correct ideas but also some inaccuracies and confusing terminology. Below is a corrected, concise explanation.

What principal rotations are
- “Principal rotations” usually means rotations about the coordinate axes (commonly called x-, y-, and z-rotations). These are represented by the rotation matrices Rx(φ), Ry(θ), Rz(ψ) that rotate by a given angle about the x-, y- or z-axis respectively.

How arbitrary 3D rotations are decomposed
- Euler’s theorem (for rotations in 3D) states: any proper rotation can be represented as a single rotation by some angle about some axis (this is the axis–angle representation).
- Equivalently, any rotation can be parameterized as a product of three rotations about coordinate axes (Euler angles). For example one common convention is
  R = Rz(α) Ry(β) Rx(γ),
  where Rx,Ry,Rz are the standard 3×3 rotation matrices. Different Euler conventions use different axis sequences (e.g. ZXZ, ZYZ, ZYX, …).
- This decomposition uses three parameters (the Euler angles). Note: the decomposition is not unique (there are multiple Euler conventions and special cases like “gimbal lock” where uniqueness/continuity fails).

Important properties and clarifications
- “Axis–angle” is not the same as “three principal rotations”: axis–angle is a single rotation about one axis; Euler-angle decompositions use three axis-aligned rotations.
- Rotations do not commute in general (Rx(α)Ry(β) ≠ Ry(β)Rx(α)), so order matters.
- Proper rotations (orientation-preserving, no reflection) form the Lie group SO(3). Composition of two rotations is another rotation (closure), the group is non-abelian.
- In 2D there is essentially one independent rotation (about the axis perpendicular to the plane). You do not need two independent axis rotations in 2D.

Example matrices
- Rx(φ) = [[1,0,0],[0,cosφ,−sinφ],[0,sinφ,cosφ]]
- Ry(θ) = [[cosθ,0,sinθ],[0,1,0],[−sinθ,0,cosθ]]
- Rz(ψ) = [[cosψ,−sinψ,0],[sinψ,cosψ,0],[0,0,1]]

Summary
- Any 3D rotation can be expressed either as one axis–angle rotation or as a product of three principal (axis-aligned) rotations (Euler angles). The latter gives a convenient parameterization but depends on axis order and is not unique.
